metadata.title: Expose The Ledger
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper development log, Week 5 — production hardening: a FastAPI HTML dashboard over the SQLite ledger, an adversarial stress-test suite, and the human-fatigue failure mode that makes visibility an architectural requirement.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal, and this video is about moving the Provenance Gatekeeper into production — with visual dashboards and adversarial stress testing. A system that catches A.I. lies is useless if human operators refuse to look at the logs. This week we pulled the data out of the terminal, and pushed the pipeline to its breaking point.
beats.new_visual_element: Cold open — a ledger nobody is reading

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Namaste, Onkar'; the question types itself into the composer
send button arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'checking who has read it…'
output lands — the ledger is full, and untouched
the last output line names the fix: EXPOSE THE LEDGER

props.command: The Gatekeeper has logged every failure for four weeks. Who on the team has actually read it?
output: evaluation_logs: 1,240 rows. Queries run by humans: 0.
A ledger behind a CLI is a ledger nobody audits.

beats.honesty_note: The 1,240 rows / 0 queries figures are ILLUSTRATIVE — no real usage telemetry was supplied. They dramatise the failure class the script names (operators not reading logs), and the reel claims no measured adoption number.

beats.narration_text: Week five was not about catching more errors. It was about making the ones we already catch impossible to ignore — and then attacking our own endpoint hard enough to find where it gives way.

Week 5 improved detection.

beats.authoring_note: Single-word trigger: BrutalistHesitantWriter matches whitespace-delimited word cores only. 'detection'->'visibility' is the reel's actual misconception — week 5 added no new detection at all.

beats.narration_text: Our production leap required two additions. First, a lightweight FastAPI HTML dashboard that queries the SQLite ledger in real time, eliminating the need for command-line access. Second, an adversarial testing suite — we deliberately bombarded our own evaluation endpoint with edge-case syntax, null values and malicious injections, to map our false-positive limits.
beats.new_visual_element: Two additions — see it, then attack it

show.event: panel 01 VISUAL DASHBOARD takes the terracotta top rule on 'First'
connector draws; panel 02 ADVERSARIAL PAYLOADS lights on 'Second' and holds
mono line lands under the band: visible, then deliberately attacked

props.sparkLine: Two additions. Neither is a feature.

beats.narration_text: So let's fire a deliberately hostile payload at our own endpoint, and watch what the dashboard does with it in real time.

show.event: composer already framed; the prompt types in
running indicator reads 'firing the stress test…'; no output lines — the next beat IS the output

props.command: Fire a SQL injection attempt mixed with unstructured text at /verify, and show me both what the normalizer does and what lands on the dashboard.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: B03 is the ask, B04 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: Watch the pipeline handle an attack. The stress test fires a deliberate S.Q.L. injection attempt, mixed with unstructured text like approx five million instead of a clean integer. Our evaluation normalizer intercepts it, safely strips the malicious characters, performs the mathematical variance check against the ChromaDB ground truth, and writes the failure straight to the dashboard.
beats.new_visual_element: The payload fires, the verdict lands on the dashboard

on 'intercepts it', the first intercepted row lands with its terracotta rule
the second row lands beneath it
on 'writes the failure', the dashboard card drops into the right panel — VERDICT: FAIL
both halves hold — intercepted at the endpoint, visible on the web route

props.sparkLine: Attacked on purpose. Flagged in public.
props.rowNote: illustrative payloads — swap in your real stress_test.py cases

beats.honesty_note: The two payload rows are ILLUSTRATIVE and captioned as such on screen — no real stress_test.py case list was supplied. The dashboard panel is a GENERIC verdict card, not a screenshot or reproduction of the project's actual HTML dashboard, which was not provided.

beats.narration_text: So where does the overall architecture fail? Human fatigue. If you force project managers to write S.Q.L. queries to audit the model's accuracy, they simply will not do it. The error ledger sits in the dark. By serving the SQLite data directly to a web route, you force the failures into the light.
beats.new_visual_element: The chain that breaks at the human, not the machine

the diagnosis lands underneath: HUMAN FATIGUE

beats.authoring_note: Reuses ThreeStageBand's failure mode with failIndex 1 of 3 — the middle stage, which exercises the travel-scaling fix made on the Week 4 reel (the token must STOP at the human step, not sail past it). The point of the beat is that the broken link is a person, not a service.

beats.narration_text: So deploy the system. Spin up the Gatekeeper with our persistent Docker Compose configuration, open the local dashboard port, and fire the adversarial test script. Watch how quickly the ledger fills with intercepted errors.
beats.new_visual_element: The two commands that stand the whole thing up

show.event: code card opens on a hard cut; traffic-light dot arms terracotta
the compose + stress-test command reveals
the dashboard URL lands beneath it
the real test lands last — watch a person read it unprompted

props.title: deploy.sh
props.code:
docker-compose up -d && python tests/stress_test.py

# then open:
#   http://localhost:8000/logs

# TASK: watch the ledger fill.

# The real test is not the row count.
# It is whether anyone opens that URL
# tomorrow without being asked.

beats.authoring_note: The closing comment is the reel's addition — it ties the task back to Scene 4's human-fatigue failure, which is the actual thesis. Without it the task measures throughput rather than the thing that broke.

beats.narration_text: And once it is running, here is the prompt worth handing a model. Give it your stress-test case list and ask what categories of hostile input you have not written a case for yet. The attacks you thought of are already handled. The gap is the ones you did not.
beats.new_visual_element: Handoff — the viewer's prompt, read aloud

show.event: composer reframes; greeting reads 'Your turn.' — the one greeting that drops the persona
prompt types in as the voice reads it verbatim
typing completes; running indicator reads 'paste this into Claude…' while the voice says what to look for

props.command: Here is my stress_test.py case list. Group my cases into categories of hostile input, then tell me which categories I have NO case for — and for each gap, write the payload that would expose it.

beats.narration_text: A ledger nobody opens is a ledger nobody has. Put the failures where people will trip over them. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
